title: MAP Architecture
subtitle: How Managed Access Providers give smaller providers every PSTN2 capability as a hosted service, without building it themselves.
endNote: PSTN2 for every provider, large or small, with each one still in control of its own numbers.

segments.text: PSTN2 needs some technical infrastructure: APIs, TLS certificates, signing keys, number discovery answers and a cache.
Large providers have engineering teams to build all of this.
But small providers, which make up most providers by number, often lack those resources.
Without help, they would be locked out of PSTN2’s benefits.
Managed Access Providers, or MAPs, solve this problem.
A MAP offers PSTN2 capabilities as a hosted service.
Small providers connect to the MAP, and the MAP handles the technical complexity.
Think of it as cloud infrastructure for telecoms.
A MAP provides the API endpoints for caller verification.
It answers number discovery queries for its customers’ numbers, including redirects for numbers they have ported out.
It runs discovery and caching for their outgoing calls.
It answers emergency location queries, manages signing and encryption keys, and offers a web portal for configuration.
Small providers get enterprise-grade infrastructure, without building it themselves.
Small providers can connect to a MAP in whichever way suits them.
A web portal, with no technical staff needed.
REST APIs, for those with some technical capability.
A SIP proxy, for traditional PBX integration.
Or pre-built connectors for popular switching platforms. MAPs meet providers where they are.
Several MAPs compete on service quality, price and features.
That makes sure providers get good value.
Unlike monopoly infrastructure, a MAP has to earn its customers, and keep them.
Competition drives innovation, and keeps costs down.
MAPs typically charge a monthly subscription, based on call volume.
For a small provider handling a few thousand calls a month, that might be £50 to £200 a month.
segments.say: For a small provider handling a few thousand calls a month, that might be fifty to two hundred pounds a month.

segments.text: That is far less than hiring engineering staff, or building the infrastructure in-house.
A MAP acts on behalf of its providers, but never controls their numbers.
Each block stays allocated to the provider in Ofcom’s lists. The MAP simply hosts the provider’s PSTN2 address and answers on its behalf.
That limits how far anyone has to trust a MAP.
If a MAP fails, calls simply fall back to today’s network. And the provider can point its Range Holder URL at another MAP.
MAPs could be licensed, and subject to regulatory oversight.
That provides accountability.
Regulators could require MAPs to meet service standards, security requirements and operational transparency.
That protects small providers from a poorly run MAP.
As more providers use MAPs, MAP services improve through economies of scale.
Better infrastructure, more features and lower costs.
Early adopters benefit too, as the ecosystem grows around them.
That creates a positive feedback loop, which accelerates adoption.
Imagine a rural provider with five thousand customers and two employees.
It could never build PSTN2 infrastructure itself.
But by subscribing to a MAP for around £100 a month, it gets the full set of PSTN2 capabilities.
segments.say: But by subscribing to a MAP for around a hundred pounds a month, it gets the full set of PSTN2 capabilities.

segments.text: Caller verification, direct routing, encryption and emergency location.
Its customers get the same benefits as those of the largest carriers.
MAPs make sure PSTN2 benefits everyone, not just the largest carriers.
Small providers can take part. Rural providers can offer modern features.
The whole telecoms ecosystem improves.
That is how a well-designed architecture opens up technology to every provider.
